sentence: It pops when it gets to about one hundred eighty degrees Celsius. Its hard shell holds the steam in, until the pressure wins.
claim: A popcorn kernel pops at about 180 °C, when steam pressure inside its hull ruptures it.
source_title: Virot and Ponomarenko, Popcorn: critical temperature, jump and sound, J. R. Soc. Interface (2015)
status: OPEN: a person must open the link and check
note: Read: 96% of kernels popped at 180 C (critical temperature close to 180 C; earlier work 177-187 C); hull bursts like a pressure vessel (about 10 bar).
derivation: A popcorn kernel pops at about 180 C, when steam pressure inside its hull ruptures it.

sentence: The pop is over in a few thousandths of a second.
claim: The pop, from the hull breaking to the kernel jumping, takes a few hundredths of a second.
source_title: Virot and Ponomarenko, Popcorn: critical temperature, jump and sound, J. R. Soc. Interface (2015)
status: OPEN: a person must open the link and check
note: Read: the abstract says popcorn "bursts open, jumps and emits a pop sound in some hundredths of a second"; high-speed frames show the fracture at 6.9 ms and the jump at 20.7 ms. Wording changed from "a few thousandths" to "about two hundredths".
derivation: The pop (the hull breaking, the starch expanding and the kernel jumping) takes some hundredths of a second (the high-speed frames put the jump near 20 ms).

claim: About two hundredths of a second, slowed 1,000 times, takes about twenty seconds on screen.
note: DERIVATION (our calculation, run it); no outside source.
derivation: About two hundredths of a second times 1,000 is about twenty seconds.

sentence: When it pops, the hole races around the film at several meters a second.
claim: The hole in a bursting soap bubble opens at a few meters a second (about 7 m/s for a very thin film).
source_title: Culick, 'Comments on a ruptured soap film', J. Appl. Phys. 31, 1128 (1960)
note: DERIVATION (our calculation, run it); no outside source. Own calculation from the standard formula; film thickness (1 micrometre) and surface tension (0.025 N/m) are assumptions, stated in our calculation. The film says 'several meters a second'.
derivation: The hole in a bursting soap film opens at the Taylor-Culick speed, v = sqrt(2 gamma / (rho h)), about 7 m/s for a 1 micrometre film with surface tension 0.025 N/m.

sentence: The whole bubble is gone in about a hundredth of a second. Here, that takes about eleven seconds.
claim: An egg-wide bubble pops in about a hundredth of a second, which is about eleven seconds when slowed 1,000 times.
note: DERIVATION (our calculation, run it); no outside source. The hole's edge runs from the puncture to the far side: half a great circle, pi R. Assumes a 1 micrometre film.
derivation: A bubble about as wide as an egg (5 cm across, R = 2.5 cm) pops in about 11 ms (pi R / v, the edge of the hole running half way round), about 11 s at 1,000x.
